À Uruk, en Mésopotamie, les premières ta: In Uruk, in Mesopotamia, the first clay tablets were used for accounting: sacks of barley, sheep, beer rations. Cuneiform writing, made of wedges pressed into clay with a reed, would later record laws, myths and the Epic of Gilgamesh. The oldest known personal name may be that of an accountant, Kushim, at the bottom of a barley receipt.
La première chose que l'humanité a écrit: The first thing humanity wrote was an invoice. The AI finds that admirably lucid.
Vers 1450, à Mayence, Johannes Gutenberg: Around 1450, in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, an oil-based ink and a screw press, perhaps inspired by wine or oil presses. His Bible came out around 1455, in about 180 copies. Movable type already existed in China, with Bi Sheng around 1040, and in Korea. But in Europe, printing made the circulation of ideas explode: some 27,500 different works printed before 1501 still survive.
Printing spread ideas. And errors, 180 copies at a time.
Diderot et d'Alembert lancent l'Encyclop: Diderot and d'Alembert launched the Encyclopédie, or Reasoned Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts and Crafts: 17 volumes of text, 11 of plates and more than 70,000 articles, published until 1772 despite two bans. The plates show trades in detail, from pin making to wig making. In 1759, the pope put it on the Index.
70 000 articles, deux interdictions et u: 70,000 articles, two bans and an angry pope. The AI thinks you have it easy.
En 1764, Diderot découvre que son librai: In 1764, Diderot discovered that his publisher had secretly censored some of his articles. Since then, the Encyclopédie has been reread with care. So will you.
